analysis.one_liner: Taxes manufacturers for using new raw materials to fund recycling programs.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 39 cosponsors and two subcommittee hearings but never got a committee vote, and died when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a fee on manufacturers — paper mills, plastics, glass container, aluminum foil, metal can, and battery makers — every time they use newly extracted ("virgin") materials instead of recycled ones, starting at $2.50 per ton in 1990 and rising to $7.50 per ton. The money would go into a new Recycling Assistance and Solid Waste Management Planning Trust Fund to pay for recycling assistance and waste-reduction programs under the Solid Waste Disposal Act. It was referred to two House committees, held hearings, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities running out of landfill space, municipalities that would receive federal recycling assistance money, and the environment generally — the fee makes recycled material relatively cheaper than newly extracted material, giving manufacturers a reason to use it, and the revenue funds local recycling and waste-reduction programs. [S2, S3]

how_it_helps.text: Charges manufacturers $2.50 per ton of virgin material in 1990, $5 in 1991, and $7.50 thereafter, so recycled inputs become cheaper relative to new ones and companies have a standing financial reason to recycle.

Routes every dollar of the fee into a dedicated Recycling Assistance and Solid Waste Management Planning Trust Fund that finances recycling assistance and a national waste-reduction clearinghouse under the Solid Waste Disposal Act.
Targets the industries behind the country's disposable packaging — paper, paperboard, plastics, glass containers, aluminum foil, metal cans, and batteries — rather than taxing the public directly.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers in the listed industries — paper mills, paperboard mills, bag and container makers, plastics producers, glass container plants, aluminum sheet and foil mills, metal can makers, and battery manufacturers — pay the fee on every ton of virgin material they use, and they would likely pass part of that cost to consumers through slightly higher prices on packaged goods. [S3]
analysis.who_pays_short: Paper, plastic, glass, can, and battery makers

drawbacks.text: The fee is built into the price of everyday packaging — paper, plastic, glass, aluminum, and cans — so consumers would pay somewhat more for packaged goods, and because lower-income households spend a larger share of their income on such goods, the cost lands harder on them than on wealthier households.

As written, the tax applies only to virgin material used in domestic manufacture; finished packaging and containers imported from abroad would face no equivalent charge, giving foreign producers a price advantage over American mills and plants.
A per-ton fee of $2.50 to $7.50 is small relative to the cost of a landfill crisis, so even supporters would acknowledge it is a modest nudge toward recycling rather than a solution on its own.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is a dedicated funding stream for recycling at a time when many communities were running out of landfill space, plus a permanent price signal favoring recycled material. The costs are real but modest: slightly higher prices on packaged goods and a competitive gap for domestic manufacturers versus untaxed imports. On balance the design is reasonable — the phase-in softens the transition and the money is earmarked rather than absorbed into general revenue — but its scale is small and the import loophole is a genuine weakness.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee — a subcommittee held two hearings in January 1990, but neither full committee ever voted to send it to the House floor, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Luken of Ohio introduced the bill on November 19, 1989, with 39 original cosponsors.

It was referred jointly to the Ways and Means Committee, which handles taxes, and the Energy and Commerce Committee; on December 11, 1989, it went to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials.
The subcommittee held hearings on January 24 and 25, 1990, but no committee or subcommittee ever voted on the bill and it never reached the House floor.
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, killing the bill with no record vote ever taken.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Paper, plastics, glass, aluminum, can, and battery manufacturers are better off because the bill died — they never faced the $7.50-per-ton fee on virgin materials. Communities got no new federal recycling funding.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Packaging manufacturers who avoided the tax

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 36 of 257 House Democrats cosponsored versus 3 of 175 House Republicans — and no vote was ever taken.

industries.note: Paper mills, paperboard mills, bag makers, and sanitary food container producers would pay the per-ton fee on every ton of virgin pulp and material they use. Their interest ran against the bill because the fee is designed to make their cheapest input — new material — more expensive.

industries.industry: Plastics, glass container, and metal can and foil producers
industries.note: Plastics materials and products, glass containers, aluminum sheet and foil, metal cans, and closures makers are all on the taxable-products list and would owe the fee per ton of virgin material. They would benefit from the bill's defeat.
Primary battery makers are listed among taxable products and would pay the fee on virgin materials used in production.

industries.industry: Recycling industry and municipal waste programs
industries.note: The trust fund would finance recycling assistance under the Solid Waste Disposal Act and support the national waste-reduction clearinghouse, and the fee would push more recycled material into the market.
